guides.title: Epistemology — The Theory of Knowledge
guides.summary: A comprehensive introduction to epistemology, the philosophical study of knowledge: what knowledge is, where it comes from, how beliefs are justified, the major theories and debates, the challenge of skepticism, and the modern branches that extend the field.

sections.heading: What Epistemology Is: The Study of Knowledge
sections.body:
Epistemology is the branch of philosophy that studies knowledge: its nature, its sources, its limits, and the standards by which beliefs count as reasonable. The word derives from the Greek episteme, meaning knowledge or understanding, and logos, meaning account or theory, so epistemology is literally the theory of knowledge. Where metaphysics asks what exists, epistemology asks how, and how well, we can know what exists. It is one of the oldest and most central areas of philosophy, because nearly every other inquiry presupposes that we can distinguish knowing from merely believing, and getting things right from getting them wrong.

Epistemologists concern themselves with several distinct kinds of questions. The most famous is the analysis question: what is knowledge, and what conditions must be met for someone to know something rather than merely believe it? A second is the source question: from what faculties or methods does knowledge arise, and how far can each be trusted, whether perception, memory, reason, testimony, or introspection? A third is the structure question: how are our justified beliefs organized, and what ultimately supports them? A fourth is the value question: why is knowledge more valuable than mere true belief? And a fifth is the skeptical question: can we know anything at all, and how do we answer the challenge that we might be radically deceived?

A useful distinction organizes the field's subject matter. Propositional knowledge, or knowledge-that, is knowledge of facts expressible in a sentence, as in knowing that water is H2O or that Paris is in France. Procedural knowledge, or knowledge-how, is a practical skill, such as knowing how to ride a bicycle or speak a language. Acquaintance knowledge is direct familiarity with a person, place, or sensation. Most of traditional epistemology concentrates on propositional knowledge, because it can be stated, evaluated for truth, and analyzed into components; the theory of skill and the theory of acquaintance are important but more specialized.

Epistemology is normative as well as descriptive. It does not only describe how people happen to form beliefs; it asks how they ought to, which beliefs are rational, which methods are reliable, and what we are entitled to accept on given evidence. In this respect it shades into logic, the philosophy of science, and the study of rationality, and it has practical stakes wherever the quality of belief matters: in courts weighing evidence, in science testing hypotheses, in journalism, medicine, and everyday judgment. Understanding epistemology means learning to ask, of any claim, not merely whether it is true but how one could know, on what basis one believes it, and how confident that basis warrants being. The sections that follow examine each of these questions in turn.

sections.heading: Knowledge as Justified True Belief
sections.body:
For much of the history of philosophy the dominant answer to the question what is knowledge has been the tripartite analysis, often called the justified-true-belief account, or JTB. On this view a person S knows that a proposition p is true if and only if three conditions are jointly satisfied: p is true, S believes that p, and S is justified in believing that p. Each condition rules out a familiar way of falling short of knowledge, and together they were long thought to capture exactly what knowledge is. The account has roots in Plato's dialogues, particularly the Theaetetus, where Socrates explores the idea that knowledge is true belief with an account or reason, though Plato himself raises difficulties for it.

Consider each condition. The truth condition holds that one cannot know something false; if you sincerely believe the earth is flat, you do not know it, because it is not so. Knowledge is factive, meaning it connects the knower to how things actually are. The belief condition holds that knowledge requires belief: you cannot know that p while failing to believe it, since knowing is a way of accepting p as true, not merely encountering the words. There are subtleties here, such as cases where people seem to know without feeling confident, but the core idea is that knowledge is a species of belief. The justification condition holds that mere true belief is not enough. A person who guesses correctly, or who believes something true for a foolish reason, has stumbled on the truth by luck and does not thereby know it. Justification is what distinguishes a well-grounded belief that happens to be true from a lucky guess.

The motivation for the justification condition is easy to feel through examples. Suppose someone believes a lottery ticket will lose purely on a whim, and it does lose; the belief is true, but we hesitate to call it knowledge because it was not held for good reasons. Or suppose a superstitious person believes it will rain because of an aching knee, and it does rain by coincidence; again, true belief without knowledge. Justification is meant to be the ingredient that connects belief to truth in a non-accidental way, so that when one knows, one gets things right not by luck but because one's belief is properly supported.

The JTB account is elegant and intuitive, and for over two thousand years it served as the standard analysis of propositional knowledge. It frames much of the field: theories of justification, debates about sources, and responses to skepticism can all be read as attempts to fill in and defend the three conditions. Yet in the twentieth century a deceptively simple set of counterexamples showed that the three conditions, even together, are not sufficient for knowledge, opening one of modern epistemology's central problems.

sections.heading: The Gettier Problem and the Analysis of Knowledge
sections.body:
In 1963 the American philosopher Edmund Gettier published a three-page paper titled Is Justified True Belief Knowledge? that overturned the settled view. Gettier presented cases in which a person has a belief that is true and justified, yet which we intuitively deny is knowledge, because the belief is true only by a lucky accident that the justification failed to track. These counterexamples showed that the three JTB conditions can all be met while knowledge is absent, so justification, truth, and belief are not jointly sufficient for knowledge.

A standard Gettier case runs as follows. Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get a job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket, so Smith justifiedly believes the proposition the person who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Unknown to Smith, he himself will get the job, and he also, by coincidence, has ten coins in his pocket. Smith's belief is true and was justified, yet it seems wrong to say he knew it, because it turned out true for reasons entirely different from those on which his justification rested. The truth was reached through a stroke of luck that the evidence did not capture. Similar cases can be multiplied endlessly: a person sees what looks like a sheep in a field and truly believes there is a sheep there, but the visible object is a dog and a real sheep is hidden behind it.

Gettier's paper launched a decades-long industry of attempts to repair the analysis of knowledge by adding a fourth condition or replacing justification altogether. One family of responses adds a no-false-lemmas condition, requiring that the belief not be inferred from any false premise; this handles some cases but not all, since Gettier-style examples can be built without inference from falsehoods. Another approach demands defeasibility, that there be no truth which, if known, would undercut the justification. A third invokes causal or tracking conditions, requiring the right sort of connection between the fact and the belief; Robert Nozick, for example, proposed that knowledge requires that one's belief be sensitive, meaning that had p been false one would not have believed it. Reliabilist theories say knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable process.

No proposed fourth condition has won consensus, and after decades some philosophers concluded that knowledge may not be analyzable into simpler necessary and sufficient conditions at all. Timothy Williamson influentially argued that knowledge is a basic, unanalyzable mental state, taking knowledge itself as fundamental rather than built from belief plus additives. Whether or not that view is right, the Gettier problem permanently reshaped epistemology, teaching that ruling out luck is central to knowledge and that the relationship between justification and truth is subtler than the tidy tripartite formula suggested.

sections.heading: The Sources of Knowledge
sections.body:
A second major question asks where knowledge comes from: through what faculties or methods do we acquire justified beliefs, and how far can each be trusted? Traditionally, epistemologists identify several basic sources, each with characteristic powers and vulnerabilities. Understanding them clarifies both how much we know and why our knowledge is fallible.

Perception, knowledge through the senses of sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell, is the richest source of information about the external world and the foundation of empirical inquiry. Yet perception is not a transparent window: illusions, hallucinations, and the theory-ladenness of observation show that the senses can mislead, and philosophers debate whether we perceive objects directly or infer them from inner sensory states. Memory preserves and delivers previously acquired knowledge; without it, knowledge could not accumulate. But memory is reconstructive and fallible, prone to distortion and confabulation, so its deliverances are trusted defeasibly rather than absolutely. Introspection gives each person seemingly privileged access to their own mental states, their pains, beliefs, and sensations. Traditionally regarded as especially secure, introspection too has limits, since people are often mistaken about their own motives and feelings.

Reason, or rational insight, is the source of knowledge that does not depend on sense experience, including logic, mathematics, and conceptual truths. Through reason we grasp that all bachelors are unmarried, that two plus three equals five, and that a valid argument transmits truth from premises to conclusion. Whether reason is a genuine independent source of substantive knowledge, or merely unpacks what is contained in our concepts, is a central dispute between rationalists and empiricists. Testimony, knowledge gained from the words of others, whether in conversation, books, teaching, or news, is the source of the overwhelming majority of what any individual knows. Almost everything you know about history, distant places, science you have not personally verified, and even your own birthdate rests on trusting others. This makes testimony indispensable but also raises hard questions about when trust is warranted, examined by social epistemology.

Epistemologists also debate whether some sources are basic and others derivative. Perception, memory, introspection, and reason are often treated as basic, providing justification non-inferentially, while testimony and inference build upon them, though some argue testimony is itself a basic source. A recurring theme is that no source is infallible: each can and does produce error. Consequently, mature epistemic practice does not rest on any single faculty but cross-checks them against one another, using perception to test testimony, reason to detect inconsistency, and memory to compare present with past. The reliability of our knowledge as a whole emerges less from the perfection of any one source than from the mutual correction of many, a point that connects the study of sources to questions about the very structure of justification.

sections.heading: The Structure of Justification
sections.body:
If our beliefs are justified by other beliefs or by evidence, a natural question arises about how this support is ultimately organized. Suppose you believe p because it is supported by q; but then what supports q? If the answer is another belief r, and r depends on yet another, we face what is called the regress problem: the chain of reasons threatens either to go on forever, to circle back on itself, or to stop somewhere. The major theories of the structure of justification are essentially different answers to this regress.

Foundationalism holds that the regress ends in basic beliefs that are justified but not by further beliefs. These foundational beliefs, perhaps immediate perceptual experiences, simple introspective reports, or self-evident rational truths, provide a bedrock on which all other justified beliefs ultimately rest, like a building standing on a foundation. Classical foundationalists such as Descartes sought foundations that were certain and indubitable; modern moderate foundationalists allow that basic beliefs can be merely prima facie justified and defeasible. The challenge for foundationalism is to explain how any belief can be justified without support from other beliefs, and how the meager foundation of immediate experience can support the vast superstructure of ordinary knowledge.

Coherentism rejects the picture of a one-directional foundation and holds instead that beliefs are justified by their mutual support, by how well they hang together in a coherent system. On this view there are no privileged basic beliefs; justification is holistic, a matter of a belief fitting consistently and explanatorily with the rest of what one believes, like the interlocking pieces of a web or the mutually supporting members of a raft rather than a pyramid on a base. Coherentism explains the interdependence of beliefs well and avoids the awkwardness of self-justifying foundations, but it faces the objection that a system could be internally coherent yet wholly detached from reality, as in a consistent but false story, and the worry that coherence permits vicious circularity.

A third option, infinitism, defended by Peter Klein, bites the bullet and accepts that justification rests on an infinite, non-repeating chain of reasons, arguing that the demand for a terminus or for circularity is what should be rejected. Infinitism is a minority view but sharpens the logical options. Some philosophers pursue hybrid positions, such as foundherentism, associated with Susan Haack, which combines a role for experience with a role for mutual support among beliefs. The debate matters because it concerns whether human knowledge has genuine anchoring in the world or floats as an internally consistent construction, and because different structures imply different diagnoses of where reasoning can go wrong. It also sets the stage for the further question of whether justification is something the knower can access from within, or something that holds in virtue of external facts about reliability.

sections.heading: Internalism, Externalism, and Reliabilism
sections.body:
A deep division in modern epistemology concerns what makes a belief justified, and specifically whether the justifying factors must be accessible to the believer's own reflection. This is the debate between internalism and externalism about justification, and it cuts across the theories of structure discussed earlier.

Internalism holds that the factors determining whether a belief is justified are internal to the believer, in the sense of being accessible through reflection, typically the person's other beliefs, evidence, and conscious mental states. On an internalist view, two people in exactly the same mental condition must be alike in what they are justified in believing, regardless of how the world outside them happens to be arranged. Justification is a matter of having good reasons that one could, at least in principle, cite and examine. This picture fits the intuitive idea that being justified means being responsible and reasonable given one's evidence, and it honors the thought that a person deceived by a convincing illusion is not thereby irrational. The classic worry for internalism is that a subject in a vivid but false experience, or a brain in a vat fed illusory inputs, would count as fully justified even though systematically wrong, so internalist justification seems to guarantee reasonableness without guaranteeing any real link to truth.

Externalism denies that all justifying factors must be internally accessible. On externalist views, whether a belief is justified can depend on facts about the believer's relation to the world that the believer need not be able to recite, above all on whether the belief was produced in a way that reliably yields truth. The leading externalist theory is reliabilism, developed especially by Alvin Goldman, according to which a belief is justified if it is produced by a reliable cognitive process, one that tends to produce true beliefs, such as normal perception, sound memory, or valid inference. A young child or an animal can then have justified beliefs, and knowledge, simply by perceiving reliably, without possessing any theory of why perception is trustworthy. Reliabilism handles many cases naturally and explains why the connection to truth matters, echoing the lesson of the Gettier problem that non-accidental correctness is central.

Externalism faces its own objections. The generality problem asks how to specify the relevant process, since any belief is produced by processes describable at many levels of breadth, with different reliabilities. The new evil demon problem presses that a systematically deceived subject seems justified even though their processes are unreliable in that deceptive world. And critics complain that reliabilism detaches justification from the believer's own perspective, allowing beliefs that are, from the inside, groundless to count as justified so long as they happen to be reliably formed. The internalism-externalism dispute remains unresolved and organizes much contemporary work, with many epistemologists concluding that the term justification may bundle together several distinct notions that different theories rightly capture.

sections.heading: Rationalism, Empiricism, and the A Priori
sections.body:
One of the oldest and most consequential debates in epistemology concerns the ultimate sources of substantive knowledge, and in particular whether the mind can know important truths about reality independently of sense experience. This is the dispute between rationalism and empiricism, and it is bound up with a set of technical distinctions that any student of the subject must master.

Central is the distinction between a priori and a posteriori knowledge. A priori knowledge is knowledge justified independently of experience, graspable by thought alone once the relevant concepts are understood, as in mathematics, logic, and truths like all triangles have three sides. A posteriori, or empirical, knowledge is justified through experience and observation, as in knowing that snow is white or that water boils at a certain temperature. A related distinction, drawn by Immanuel Kant, separates analytic from synthetic propositions: analytic truths are those whose predicate is contained in the subject, true by meaning alone, such as all bachelors are unmarried, whereas synthetic truths say something substantive beyond the mere analysis of concepts.

Rationalists, in a tradition running through Plato, Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz, hold that reason is a source of significant knowledge about reality, and that some of what we know is both a priori and substantive. Descartes sought to rebuild all knowledge on rational foundations discovered by pure thought, and Leibniz held that the necessary truths of mathematics and metaphysics are grasped by the intellect rather than read off the senses. Rationalists often invoke innate ideas or rational intuition and argue that experience alone cannot account for the necessity and universality of mathematical and logical knowledge. Empiricists, in the line of Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, counter that the mind begins as a blank slate and that all our ideas and knowledge derive ultimately from sense experience. Locke attacked innate ideas; Hume argued that any claim about the world beyond present experience, including causation, rests on habit and observation rather than pure reason, and famously drew a sharp line between relations of ideas and matters of fact.

Kant sought a synthesis, arguing that there are synthetic a priori truths, substantive yet knowable independently of experience, made possible because the mind actively structures all experience through built-in forms and categories, so that space, time, and causation are contributed by the knowing subject. In the twentieth century, empiricist logical positivists tried to eliminate the synthetic a priori, treating a priori truths as merely analytic, while W. V. O. Quine, in Two Dogmas of Empiricism, attacked the very analytic-synthetic distinction and argued that no belief is immune from revision in light of experience. The debate persists in new forms, and its stakes are high: it concerns whether human beings can, by thinking, reach truths about the deep structure of reality, or whether all genuine knowledge must ultimately answer to observation.

sections.heading: Skepticism and the Problem of the External World
sections.body:
Skepticism, the view that we lack knowledge, or cannot attain it, in some domain or across the board, is not merely a nuisance but a driving force of epistemology, because meeting the skeptical challenge forces theories of knowledge to justify themselves. Skeptical arguments are powerful precisely because they use ordinary standards of knowledge to reach the extraordinary conclusion that we know almost nothing.

Ancient skepticism took two main forms. Academic skeptics held that knowledge is unattainable, while the Pyrrhonists, following Sextus Empiricus, refused even to assert that, recommending suspension of judgment as the path to tranquility. The Pyrrhonists developed modes, or standard argument patterns, exploiting the conflict of appearances, the relativity of perception, and the regress of justification to show that for any claim an equally strong opposing case can be mounted, so the wise response is to withhold assent. Their goal was practical peace of mind rather than a positive doctrine, a therapeutic rather than merely theoretical skepticism.

Modern skepticism is usually associated with Rene Descartes, who in his Meditations deployed radical doubt as a method. Descartes noted that the senses sometimes deceive, that dreaming can be indistinguishable from waking, and finally imagined an evil demon of great power devoting itself to deceiving him about everything, even simple mathematics. The upshot is the problem of the external world: how can I know that there is a physical world at all, rather than that I am being systematically deceived? Descartes sought to escape by way of the one thing he could not doubt, his own existence as a thinking thing, captured in the cogito, I think therefore I am, and then tried to rebuild knowledge on the guarantee of a non-deceiving God, a move widely regarded as unsuccessful. The modern version replaces the demon with the brain in a vat, a brain kept alive and fed computer-generated experiences indistinguishable from ordinary life; since your experience would be identical whether you are an embodied person or such a brain, how can you rule the second possibility out?

Responses are numerous. G. E. Moore simply insisted that he knew he had hands, treating this as more certain than any skeptical premise, and turned the argument around. Contextualists such as Keith DeRose argue that knowledge is context-sensitive, so that ordinary claims to know are true in everyday contexts while skeptical scenarios raise the standards in the philosophy seminar, dissolving the apparent contradiction. Externalists reply that if our beliefs are in fact reliably produced, we have knowledge whether or not we can refute the skeptic from the inside. Others accept a measure of fallibilism, holding that knowledge does not require the impossibility of error, only that error be suitably ruled out. Few philosophers are genuine global skeptics, but nearly all agree that saying exactly what is wrong with the skeptical argument is far harder than it first appears, which is why skepticism remains a permanent test of every epistemology.

sections.heading: Theories of Truth
sections.body:
Because knowledge requires truth, epistemology is intertwined with the question of what truth itself is. To say a belief is true seems obvious in individual cases, yet philosophers disagree sharply about what truth consists in, and the competing theories carry different implications for how belief connects to the world. This is strictly a topic in metaphysics and the philosophy of language as much as epistemology, but no theory of knowledge is complete without a view about it.

The correspondence theory, the most intuitive and historically dominant, holds that a belief or statement is true when it corresponds to, or matches, the way the world actually is. The statement snow is white is true because, in reality, snow is white; truth is a relation of agreement between a representation and a fact. This theory captures the common-sense idea that truth is about getting reality right and that facts are independent of what anyone believes. Its difficulties lie in specifying what facts are and what the correspondence relation amounts to, especially for negative, general, or abstract truths, and in explaining how we could ever compare a belief with an unconceptualized world.

The coherence theory holds instead that truth consists in a belief's coherence with a comprehensive, consistent system of beliefs. On this view, associated with some idealists such as Bradley and Blanshard, there is no comparing beliefs with a bare reality outside all thought; a belief is true insofar as it fits harmoniously into the maximally coherent whole. Coherence theories connect naturally to coherentist theories of justification but face the objection that more than one internally coherent system might exist, and that coherence seems better suited to being a test of truth than its very nature. The pragmatic theory, developed by Charles Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, ties truth to inquiry and practice: for Peirce, truth is the ideal endpoint on which inquiry would converge, and for James true beliefs are, roughly, those that prove useful and reliable to act upon. Pragmatism usefully links truth to verification and consequence but is criticized for seeming to conflate what is true with what is merely useful to believe.

Deflationary theories take a different tack, denying that truth is a substantive property needing analysis at all. On the redundancy or minimalist view, associated with Frank Ramsey and Paul Horwich, to say it is true that snow is white says no more than that snow is white; the truth predicate is merely a device of endorsement and generalization, letting us affirm claims without restating them. Deflationism dissolves rather than answers the traditional question. The choice among these theories shapes epistemology profoundly, since what one takes truth to be constrains what it could mean for our beliefs to reach it, and whether the goal of inquiry is correspondence to a mind-independent world, coherence within thought, success in practice, or nothing over and above asserting our claims.

sections.heading: Social Epistemology, Testimony, and Disagreement
sections.body:
Traditional epistemology often pictured the knower as a solitary individual, weighing evidence in isolation, but most of what anyone knows depends on other people. Social epistemology studies the collective and interpersonal dimensions of knowledge: how we learn from testimony, how communities and institutions produce and transmit knowledge, and how we should respond when others disagree with us. It has become one of the most active areas of the field, with obvious relevance to science, education, journalism, and public life.

The epistemology of testimony asks when it is rational to believe what others tell us. Since you cannot personally verify most of what you know, from historical facts to scientific results to the reliability of your own name, testimony is indispensable, yet it seems to let you acquire knowledge secondhand. Reductionists, following Hume, argue that trust in testimony is justified only by your own evidence that testimony is generally reliable, so testimonial knowledge reduces to inductive support from experience. Anti-reductionists, following Thomas Reid, counter that testimony is a basic source: we are entitled to believe what we are told unless we have specific reason to doubt it, much as we are entitled to trust perception. Between these lie many nuanced positions, and the debate matters because it determines how demanding rational trust should be and how vulnerable we are to misinformation.

Social epistemology also examines the structures through which knowledge is produced, especially science, treating peer review, replication, expert consensus, and the division of cognitive labor as epistemic institutions whose design affects how reliably truth emerges. It studies the identification of experts by non-experts, a pressing everyday problem, and the epistemic effects of trust, authority, and the internet. A related body of work, feminist and standpoint epistemology, argues that social position and power shape what questions get asked, whose testimony is credited, and what counts as knowledge, and introduces the influential notion of epistemic injustice, developed by Miranda Fricker, whereby people are wronged specifically in their capacity as knowers, for instance when a speaker's credibility is unfairly discounted because of prejudice.

The epistemology of disagreement asks how you should revise your confidence when an epistemic peer, someone equally informed and capable, disagrees with you. Conciliationists argue that peer disagreement should reduce your confidence, since the mere fact that a competent equal reaches the opposite conclusion is evidence you may be mistaken. Steadfast theorists reply that you may rationally retain your view, since you have access to your own reasoning in a way you do not have to the peer's. The question bears directly on intellectual humility, political polarization, and the rationality of holding firm or yielding in the face of dissent. Together these strands show that knowledge is not merely a relation between an individual mind and the world but a social achievement, shaped by trust, testimony, institutions, and the distribution of credibility across a community.

sections.heading: Naturalized, Virtue, and Formal Epistemology
sections.body:
Twentieth- and twenty-first-century epistemology branched into several distinctive programs that reconceive how the theory of knowledge should be pursued. Three of the most influential are naturalized epistemology, virtue epistemology, and formal epistemology, each offering a different vision of the subject.

Naturalized epistemology, launched by W. V. O. Quine in his 1969 essay Epistemology Naturalized, argues that the traditional project of justifying knowledge from an armchair, on purely a priori foundations, has failed, and that epistemology should instead become continuous with empirical science, especially psychology. On this view, we should study how human beings actually form beliefs, how sensory input produces theory, and which cognitive processes are in fact reliable, rather than seeking an impossible foundational certification of knowledge from outside science. Critics object that a purely descriptive study of belief-formation abandons epistemology's essential normative task of saying how we ought to reason, not merely how we do; defenders reply that norms can be recovered from the study of which processes reliably attain our cognitive goals. Naturalism has deeply influenced the field, encouraging attention to cognitive science, evolutionary considerations, and empirical findings about reasoning and bias.

Virtue epistemology shifts the primary focus from the properties of beliefs to the qualities of the believer, taking intellectual virtues as central. Just as virtue ethics evaluates actions by reference to the character of the agent, virtue epistemology evaluates beliefs by reference to the intellectual character of the knower. Reliabilist virtue theorists, such as Ernest Sosa, treat intellectual virtues as stable, reliable cognitive faculties or competences, and analyze knowledge as apt belief, belief that is true because it manifests the knower's competence, an approach that neatly diagnoses Gettier cases as belief that is accurate but not through competence. Responsibilist virtue theorists, such as Linda Zagzebski, emphasize acquired character traits like open-mindedness, intellectual courage, thoroughness, and honesty, connecting epistemology to education and the cultivation of good inquirers. Virtue epistemology has proven fertile for understanding understanding, wisdom, and the value of knowledge.

Formal epistemology brings the tools of logic, probability, and decision theory to bear on epistemic questions, treating degrees of belief, or credences, rather than all-or-nothing belief, as fundamental. Its central framework is Bayesian, representing a rational agent's confidence as probabilities that obey the axioms of the probability calculus and that are updated on new evidence by conditionalization, formalized in Bayes's theorem. This approach illuminates confirmation, evidence, and how much a finding should shift belief, and it underlies much of statistics and the modern philosophy of science. It faces questions about where prior probabilities come from, how idealized rational agents relate to real thinkers, and how graded credence connects to ordinary talk of knowledge and belief. Together, these three programs show epistemology as a living, evolving discipline, drawing on science, ethics, and mathematics rather than resting on a single fixed method.

sections.heading: Misconceptions and Where Epistemology Connects Onward
sections.body:
Several persistent misconceptions distort popular thinking about knowledge, and clearing them away is part of what studying epistemology accomplishes. A first is the confusion of knowledge with certainty. Many assume that to know something one must be absolutely certain, immune from any possibility of error, so that any conceivable doubt shows we do not really know. Most epistemologists reject this: they are fallibilists, holding that one can know something while it remains logically possible that one is mistaken, since requiring certainty would collapse into the very skepticism the equation was meant to avoid. Knowledge asks for adequate grounding and non-accidental truth, not the impossibility of error.

A second misconception treats all opinions as epistemically equal, sliding from the true observation that people disagree to the false conclusion that no belief is better justified than another. Epistemology is precisely the study of the standards that make some beliefs more reasonable, better supported, and more likely true than others; recognizing fallibility is not the same as embracing a relativism in which evidence and argument make no difference. A third confuses the psychological question of what causes a belief with the normative question of what justifies it: that a belief was produced by upbringing or emotion neither guarantees nor precludes that it is well justified, and the genetic origin of a belief must be separated from its rational credentials. A fourth mistakes knowing-that for knowing-how, or assumes that being able to state a rule is the same as possessing a skill, when the two can come apart entirely.

Properly understood, epistemology is not idle wordplay but a discipline with pervasive practical stakes. It underwrites the philosophy of science, which asks how evidence confirms theories and what makes a method rational, and it shapes debates about expertise, testimony, and misinformation that determine how a society sustains reliable belief. It informs law, where standards of proof, the weighing of testimony, and reasonable doubt are epistemic notions; medicine, where diagnosis is inference under uncertainty; and education, whose aim is the cultivation of good inquirers. In an age of information overload, algorithmic curation, and coordinated deception, the epistemological questions of when to trust a source, how to weigh conflicting evidence, and how confident to be have become urgently practical.

Epistemology also connects to the rest of philosophy. It borders metaphysics through the question of truth and the nature of the reality we seek to know; it borders ethics through the norms of belief, intellectual virtue, and the responsibilities of the inquirer; it borders logic and the philosophy of mind through the analysis of reasoning, evidence, and mental states; and it borders the philosophy of language through the vehicles by which knowledge is expressed and communicated. To think clearly about knowledge, in the end, is to learn to ask of any claim not only whether it is true but how one could know, on what basis one believes it, and how much confidence that basis can bear, a habit of mind that is among the most valuable philosophy can teach.

guides.title: Metaphysics — The Study of What Exists
guides.summary: An introduction to metaphysics, the branch of philosophy that asks what fundamentally exists and what reality is like: its history, its central problems of being, universals, identity, causation, time, freedom, possibility and mind, and the criticisms it has faced.

sections.heading: What Metaphysics Is and Its Place in Philosophy
sections.body: Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that inquires into the most fundamental nature of reality: what there is, what it is like at bottom, and what the most general features of existence are. Where the special sciences each study some particular domain, physics the physical, biology the living, economics the exchange of goods, metaphysics asks questions that lie beneath and across all of them. It asks not what particular things exist but what it is for anything to exist at all; not what causes a specific event but what causation itself is; not whether a given object has changed but what change and persistence are. These are questions that no experiment can straightforwardly settle, because they concern the framework within which experiments are interpreted rather than any measurable quantity, and yet they are unavoidable the moment one begins to think carefully about the world. A helpful way to grasp the subject is through its classic questions. Do numbers exist, or only the things we count? When a river flows on and every drop is replaced, in what sense is it the same river? Is the future already fixed, or genuinely open? Are you the same person you were as a child, and what makes you so? Could things have been otherwise than they are, and what grounds such possibilities? Is the mind simply the brain, or something more? Each of these is a metaphysical question, and each has been debated for millennia without the kind of consensus that mature sciences achieve, which is part of what makes metaphysics both frustrating and perennially alive. Metaphysics sits alongside the other great divisions of philosophy and is intertwined with them. Epistemology asks how and whether we can know things; metaphysics asks what there is to be known. Logic supplies the tools of valid inference that metaphysical arguments must respect. Ethics and aesthetics presuppose metaphysical views about persons, values and freedom. Because metaphysics concerns the most general structure of reality, its conclusions ripple outward into every other area of thought, which is why thinkers as different as Plato, Aristotle, Aquinas, Descartes, Leibniz, Hume and Kant all found they could not avoid it. The word itself, as the next section explains, arose from an accident of editing, but the enterprise it names is as old as systematic thought. It is worth stressing at the outset that metaphysics is not a matter of arbitrary opinion or mystical pronouncement; its practitioners aim to argue rigorously, to define their terms with care, to consider objections, and to weigh competing theories by such standards as consistency, explanatory power and economy, the same intellectual virtues prized in the sciences. What distinguishes it is only that its subject matter is the most general and fundamental, so that observation alone cannot decide its questions. To study metaphysics is to take seriously the strange fact that the world exists at all and to try, with argument rather than dogma, to say something true about its deepest character.

sections.heading: The Origins: Aristotle and First Philosophy
sections.body: The word metaphysics has one of the most curious origins of any term in philosophy, and the story is worth telling because it corrects a common misunderstanding. Aristotle, working in the fourth century before the common era, wrote a series of treatises on a subject he did not call metaphysics at all. He called it first philosophy, and sometimes theology or wisdom, and he described it as the study of being qua being, that is, the study of things simply insofar as they exist, abstracting from their particular characters as physical or living or human. He also treated it as the search for the first causes and principles of everything, the most general and hence the most fundamental knowledge. These were the deepest and most abstract of his inquiries. The name we use came later and by chance. In the first century before the common era, the editor Andronicus of Rhodes arranged Aristotle's works for publication. He placed these treatises on first philosophy immediately after Aristotle's treatises on nature, the Physics. In Greek, after the physics is ta meta ta physika, and this positional label, meaning simply the books that come after the Physics, hardened into the name of the discipline. So metaphysics did not originally mean beyond the physical or the supernatural, as popular usage now often assumes; it meant, literally, the volumes shelved after the physics. That the accidental name happened to suggest something lying beyond nature was a happy coincidence that later ages read into it. Aristotle's own conception nonetheless set the agenda for centuries. He distinguished substance, the independently existing things such as a particular horse or man, from the properties and relations that depend on substances, and he argued that being is said in many ways, so that existence is not a single uniform notion. He developed the doctrine of the four causes, the analysis of potentiality and actuality, and the idea of an unmoved mover as the ultimate source of motion, which fed into later theology. Through the medieval period, especially in the hands of Thomas Aquinas and the Islamic philosophers Avicenna and Averroes, this Aristotelian metaphysics became the shared framework of educated thought, the scaffolding on which questions about God, soul and creation were hung. Even philosophers who rebelled against Aristotle, and there were many in the modern period, defined themselves partly against his metaphysics. It is a striking irony that the discipline's very name would have been unfamiliar to the man who did most to establish it, and that its suggestion of the supernatural, which has coloured popular usage down to the present, was no part of his intent. To understand where the subject came from, and why its questions take the shape they do, one must begin with this founder who never used its name.

sections.heading: Ontology: The Question of Being and Existence
sections.body: At the heart of metaphysics lies ontology, the study of being and existence, which asks the deceptively simple question: what is there? One might expect a short answer, everything, but the interest lies in the disputes over what belongs on the list. Almost everyone agrees that ordinary physical objects such as tables, trees and planets exist. But do numbers and mathematical objects exist, and if so, where and in what sense, given that we never bump into the number seven? Do properties such as redness exist over and above the red things? Do fictional characters, holes, shadows, events, possibilities or the past exist? Ontology tries to draw up a principled inventory of the fundamental kinds of things, an account of the basic categories of being, and to defend it against rivals who would add or subtract entries. A central ontological divide is between those who populate the world richly and those who prefer desert landscapes, to borrow a phrase associated with the twentieth-century philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine. Ontological economy, often invoked under the name of Ockham's razor after the medieval thinker William of Ockham, counsels that we should not multiply entities beyond necessity, admitting only what we must to explain the phenomena. Against this pull toward parsimony stands the worry that too spare an ontology leaves us unable to account for mathematics, morality, or the truths of ordinary talk. Much metaphysical argument consists in weighing the theoretical cost of admitting some kind of entity against the cost of doing without it. Quine gave the modern discussion a sharp tool with his slogan that to be is to be the value of a bound variable. The idea is that we can read a theory's ontological commitments off the logical form of the statements it holds true: if a theory, when regimented into formal logic, must quantify over certain things, say over numbers, in order to state its truths, then it is committed to their existence. Ontology becomes, on this view, a matter of deciding which of our best theories to accept and then acknowledging honestly what those theories say there is. Others resist this linguistic turn, insisting that existence is a substantive matter not settled by how we choose to talk. There are also deep puzzles about existence itself: whether it is a genuine property that things have, a question Kant pressed against arguments for God's existence, or whether, as many logicians hold, existence is not a predicate of individuals at all but a matter of something falling under a concept. Ontology thus reaches from the homeliest catalogue of furniture to the most abstract questions about what it even means to say that something is.

sections.heading: Universals and Particulars: The Problem of Properties
sections.body: Look around and you will notice that many distinct things share features: countless separate objects are red, are round, or are electrons. This everyday fact poses one of the oldest problems in metaphysics, the problem of universals. When two roses are both red, is there some single thing, redness, that they both possess and that somehow exists in each of them at once? Or are there only the individual red roses, with the word red merely a convenient label we apply to resembling particulars? A universal is understood as something that can be wholly present in many places at the same time and shared by many things; a particular is a single, located individual. The debate concerns whether universals are real additions to the world's inventory, and it has divided philosophers since antiquity. The realist answers yes, universals exist. Plato held the most dramatic version: the Forms, such as Redness, Beauty and Justice, exist in a timeless, non-physical realm, more real than the fleeting physical things that merely participate in them and so acquire their characters. Aristotle, his pupil, offered a more down-to-earth realism, agreeing that universals are real but insisting they exist only in the particular things that instantiate them, not in a separate heaven. This contrast between transcendent and immanent realism has echoed through the centuries. Realists argue that only shared universals can explain genuine resemblance, the objectivity of scientific classification, and the truth of general statements. The nominalist answers no; only particulars exist, and universals are in some sense a fiction of language or thought. Medieval nominalists such as William of Ockham held that generality belongs to words and concepts, not to the world: there is no redness, only red things and the name red that we extend to them by their resemblance. Modern nominalists have developed more sophisticated versions. Some appeal to classes or sets of particulars; some, the trope theorists, accept that each red thing has its own particular redness, an individual property or trope, and explain shared character as the exact resemblance of these distinct tropes rather than the sharing of one universal. Conceptualism takes a middle path, locating universality in the mind's concepts. Each view pays a price. Extreme nominalism struggles to ground objective resemblance without smuggling in a universal of similarity; realism must explain the strange mode of being of things that can be wholly in many places at once. That the problem remains genuinely open, with able defenders on every side, makes it a model of how metaphysical disputes can be sharpened for centuries without being closed, and a gateway to nearly every other topic in the field.

sections.heading: Identity, Change and Persistence Through Time
sections.body: Ordinary objects persist through change: a tree grows, loses leaves and gains rings yet remains the same tree; you age, replace nearly every cell, and remain you. Metaphysics finds this commonplace deeply puzzling, and the puzzle has a famous emblem in the Ship of Theseus. As the ship's planks rot they are replaced one by one until no original plank remains; is it still the same ship? Now suppose the discarded planks are reassembled into a ship; which of the two, if either, is the original? The tale dramatizes the tension between identity, which logic treats as strict, and the loose, gradual sameness we attribute to changing things. Heraclitus pressed the same point with his remark that one cannot step into the same river twice, since fresh waters ever flow. Philosophers distinguish two senses of identity to make progress. Qualitative identity is exact similarity: two new coins off the same press are qualitatively identical. Numerical identity is being one and the same thing: the coin in my pocket now is numerically identical with the coin I put there this morning, though it may have acquired a scratch and so ceased to be qualitatively the same as before. Change is precisely the situation in which something is numerically one and the same while becoming qualitatively different over time. A guiding principle, Leibniz's Law or the indiscernibility of identicals, states that if two things are numerically identical they share all their properties; the challenge is to reconcile this with the fact that a changing thing has incompatible properties, straight then bent, at different times. Two broad theories of persistence answer this challenge. Endurantism holds that an object is wholly present at each moment of its existence; the whole tree exists now and existed yesterday, and it has its properties at times, being straight-at-noon and bent-at-dusk, so no contradiction arises. Perdurantism holds instead that objects are extended through time as well as space, made up of temporal parts or stages the way a road is made of spatial parts; the tree is a four-dimensional whole, and it is straight in virtue of its noon-part and bent in virtue of its dusk-part. Related debates concern material constitution, as when a statue and the lump of clay it is made from seem to be one object yet have different properties and histories, and personal identity, the question of what makes a person at one time the same as a person at another. John Locke influentially tied personal identity to continuity of memory and consciousness rather than to sameness of body or soul, opening problems about amnesia, duplication and survival that remain vigorously debated and that connect metaphysics directly to questions about the self, death and moral responsibility.

sections.heading: Substance, Objects and the Bundle Theory
sections.body: When we speak of a thing, an apple, a stone, a person, we seem to distinguish the thing itself from its properties: the apple is red, round, sweet and firm, yet it is not identical with any one of these, nor simply their sum, for it is what has them. This intuition gives rise to one of the most persistent notions in metaphysics, that of substance. In the broadest traditional sense, a substance is a fundamental, independently existing thing, a bearer of properties that does not itself depend on inhering in something else. Aristotle contrasted primary substances, individual things like this particular horse, with the qualities, quantities and relations that can only exist by belonging to substances. Substance, on this picture, is the basic furniture of the world, and everything else is a modification of it. But what exactly is the substance, once we strip away all its properties? Here philosophers divide sharply. On one view, associated with John Locke, there must be a substratum, a bare particular or underlying subject that has the properties but is not itself any of them, holding them together and grounding the object's identity. Locke himself was uneasy about this, calling the substratum a something-we-know-not-what, since by hypothesis it has no properties of its own by which we might grasp it, and critics have pressed that a propertyless bearer is at best mysterious and at worst incoherent. If we can never encounter or characterize it, what work is it really doing? The rival bundle theory, whose most famous proponent is David Hume, dispenses with the substratum altogether and holds that an object simply is a bundle of its properties, co-located and bound together, with nothing underneath. The apple is the collection of its redness, roundness, sweetness and the rest, unified by their all occurring together; there is no additional bare thing that has them. This ontology is more economical and avoids the mysterious substratum, but it faces its own difficulties. It must explain what binds the properties into one object rather than a mere list, a relation sometimes called compresence. It struggles with the possibility of two distinct objects sharing all their properties, since if an object just is its bundle of properties, two exactly similar things would collapse into one, which seems wrong. And it must account for change, since as properties come and go the bundle changes, threatening the object's identity over time. The debate between substratum and bundle theories, like the debate over universals to which it is closely linked, shows how the analysis of something as familiar as a physical object opens onto fundamental and unresolved questions about the structure of reality.

sections.heading: Causation and the Nature of Laws
sections.body: That some things bring about others is among our most basic convictions: the brick breaks the window, the heat boils the water, the vote elects the candidate. Yet when metaphysicians ask what causation actually is, the confident notion dissolves into difficulty. Aristotle offered an early and influential analysis in his doctrine of the four causes, distinguishing the material cause, what a thing is made of; the formal cause, its shape or organizing pattern; the efficient cause, what brings it about; and the final cause, the end or purpose for which it exists. Modern usage narrows cause largely to Aristotle's efficient cause, but his broader scheme reminds us that explanation comes in several kinds, and the banishment of final causes from physics was itself a major intellectual event of the scientific revolution. The sharpest modern challenge came from David Hume in the eighteenth century. When we watch one billiard ball strike another and set it moving, Hume observed, we see the first ball's motion, the contact, and the second ball's motion, but we never perceive any additional ingredient of causal power or necessary connection binding them. All we ever actually observe is that events of one kind are regularly followed by events of another. Hume concluded that our idea of causation reduces to constant conjunction plus the habit of expectation the mind forms after repeated experience; the felt necessity is a projection of our expectations, not something read off the world. This deflationary account, the regularity theory, threatens to make causation far thinner than we suppose. Later philosophers, unsatisfied that causation is mere regularity, since some regularities are accidental and some causes act but once, have sought better accounts. The counterfactual theory, developed influentially by David Lewis in the twentieth century, analyses causation in terms of what would have happened otherwise: roughly, the brick caused the window to break because, had the brick not struck it, the window would not have broken. Other theories appeal to the transfer of a physical quantity such as energy or momentum, or to probability-raising, the cause making its effect more likely. Closely bound up with causation is the question of laws of nature. Are laws merely the most sweeping regularities that happen to hold, as a Humean holds, so that the universe simply exhibits certain patterns with no deeper necessity? Or do laws express a genuine necessity, a real relation between properties that governs what must happen, as necessitarian theorists such as Armstrong, Dretske and Tooley have argued? On the answer hangs whether the world is, at bottom, a mosaic of loose events or a system bound by objective necessities, a question that shapes how we understand science itself.

sections.heading: Space, Time and the Metaphysics of Physics
sections.body: Space and time are so pervasive that we rarely think to ask what they are, yet metaphysics has debated their nature for centuries, and the debate now runs in close conversation with physics. A foundational question is whether space and time are substances in their own right or merely relations among things. The substantivalist, whose great champion was Isaac Newton, holds that space and time are a real container, an absolute stage that exists independently of the objects and events within it and would persist even if emptied of all matter. Newton argued that absolute space was needed to make sense of true motion and, famously, of the forces that appear in rotation. The relationalist, whose great champion was Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, denies this, holding that space is nothing but the system of spatial relations among bodies and time nothing but the order of successive events; talk of empty absolute space is, for Leibniz, empty indeed. Their disagreement was sharpened in the celebrated Leibniz-Clarke correspondence, where Leibniz argued that an absolute space would leave God no reason to place the universe here rather than there, offending the principle that nothing happens without a sufficient reason. Time raises further puzzles distinctively its own. One concerns which times are real. Presentism holds that only the present exists; the past has gone and the future is not yet, so reality is confined to a moving now. Eternalism holds that past, present and future are all equally real, differing only in their position, much as distant places are real though not here; on this block-universe view, time is like a fourth dimension laid out alongside space. A third view, the growing-block theory, holds that the past and present are real but the future is not, so reality accumulates as time passes. These are not idle options, for they bear on whether the passage of time is an objective feature of the world or an artefact of our perspective. The philosopher John McTaggart pressed the issue with a notorious argument that time is unreal. He distinguished the A-series, which orders events as past, present and future, from the B-series, which orders them merely as earlier and later. Change, he argued, requires the A-series, since only the shifting of events from future to present to past is genuine becoming; yet the A-series is contradictory, because every event is past, present and future, and the attempt to relativize these to times only regenerates the problem. Whatever one makes of McTaggart's reasoning, it forced clarity about what temporal passage involves. Modern physics has transformed these debates: Einstein's relativity, by making simultaneity relative to a frame of reference and welding space and time into a single spacetime, is widely read as favouring eternalism over presentism and relationalism over naive absolutism, though the philosophical interpretation of the physics remains contested.

sections.heading: Free Will, Determinism and Agency
sections.body: Few metaphysical questions touch human life as directly as that of free will, for on it seem to hang our practices of praise and blame, punishment and reward, and our very sense of ourselves as agents. The problem arises from a clash between two things we are inclined to believe. On one side is the intuition that we act freely, that when we choose we could genuinely have done otherwise, and that we are the authors of our deeds. On the other side is determinism, the thesis that every event, including every human choice, is the inevitable outcome of prior causes according to the laws of nature, so that given the state of the world long before your birth, everything you do was already fixed. If determinism is true, how can any of your choices be free, and how can you be responsible for them? Positions on this problem are usually sorted by two questions: is determinism true, and is free will compatible with it? The hard determinist answers that determinism is true and that it leaves no room for free will, so free will is an illusion and our ordinary notions of moral responsibility must be revised. The libertarian, at the opposite pole, insists that we do have genuine free will and concludes that determinism must therefore be false, at least for human choices; some libertarians appeal to a special kind of agent causation, in which the self originates action without being determined by prior events, and some have hoped that indeterminism at the quantum level might make room for freedom, though mere randomness seems to secure caprice rather than control. Between these stands compatibilism, historically the most popular position among philosophers, which holds that free will and determinism can both be true because they are not really in conflict. The compatibilist, in a tradition running through Hobbes and Hume to the present, redefines freedom not as the metaphysical power to have done otherwise in an uncaused way, but as acting according to one's own desires and reasons without external compulsion or constraint. On this view a person acts freely when their action flows from their own will, even if that will was itself caused; the drug addict acting on a craving they disown is unfree, while the deliberating agent following their own considered judgment is free, whatever the causal history. Critics, most forcefully Peter van Inwagen with his consequence argument, reply that if our actions are the consequences of laws and a past we did not control, then in the deepest sense they are not up to us, and the compatibilist has merely changed the subject. The debate remains open, entangling metaphysics with ethics, psychology and the science of the brain.

sections.heading: Modality: Possibility, Necessity and Possible Worlds
sections.body: Some truths seem to hold not just as a matter of fact but as a matter of necessity, while other things, though false, seem genuinely possible. It is a fact that you are reading this, but you could have been elsewhere; it is necessary that two plus two equals four, and impossible that a triangle have four sides. This dimension of reality, concerning what must be, what may be and what cannot be, is called modality, and it is one of the subtlest areas of metaphysics. Modal notions pervade ordinary and scientific thought, in talk of what would happen under different conditions, of dispositions such as fragility, of laws that could not be violated, and of abilities and chances. But what grounds these modal facts? In virtue of what is something merely possible rather than actual, or necessary rather than contingent? A powerful framework for analysing modality speaks of possible worlds. A possible world is a complete way things could have been; the actual world is one such way, the way things in fact are, and the other possible worlds represent alternative total scenarios. On this scheme, to say something is possible is to say it is true in some possible world, and to say it is necessary is to say it is true in all of them. This apparatus, whose roots reach back to Leibniz's idea that God surveyed all possible worlds and created the best, was made precise in twentieth-century logic and proved enormously fruitful. But it raises the question of what possible worlds themselves are. David Lewis defended the startling view called modal realism, that other possible worlds are just as real and concrete as our own, vast physical universes spatiotemporally disconnected from ours, differing from the actual world only in that we happen to inhabit this one. Most philosophers found this ontological extravagance too much to accept and preferred various forms of ersatzism, treating possible worlds as abstract objects, maximal consistent sets of propositions or states of affairs, rather than concrete places. The philosopher Saul Kripke transformed modal metaphysics with his lectures published as Naming and Necessity. He argued that some necessary truths can be known only through experience, breaking the long-assumed link between the necessary and the knowable-in-advance: that water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen, once discovered, is necessary, for nothing lacking that composition would be water, yet it was learned empirically. He distinguished necessity, a metaphysical matter of how things must be, from the a priori, an epistemic matter of what can be known independently of experience, and defended the idea of essential properties that a thing could not have lacked while remaining itself. These distinctions, together with the possible-worlds framework, gave metaphysicians precise tools to discuss essence, identity across possibilities and the modal structure of the world, and they revitalized a subject that earlier skeptics had tried to dismiss as meaningless.

sections.heading: Mind, Matter and the Metaphysics of Consciousness
sections.body: Among the things that exist are minds, and their place in the natural order is one of metaphysics' hardest problems. You are directly acquainted with your own conscious experience, the felt redness of red, the ache of pain, the stream of thought, and yet the world revealed by physics seems to consist of colourless particles and fields governed by mathematical laws. How does conscious experience fit into that world? Is the mind simply the brain, or something distinct from it? This is the mind-body problem, and the various answers to it map onto the deepest divisions in metaphysics between the material and the immaterial. The most famous dualist answer is that of René Descartes, who held that mind and body are two utterly different kinds of substance: the body extended in space and governed by mechanical law, the mind an unextended thinking thing. Substance dualism honours the apparent gulf between thought and matter but faces the notorious problem of interaction, how an immaterial mind could push around a material brain, and where in the causal order of physics such influence would enter. At the opposite extreme stands materialism or physicalism, now the majority view among philosophers and scientists, which holds that everything, including the mind, is ultimately physical; mental states are states of the brain, whether identical with particular neural configurations or realized by them much as software is realized in hardware. Between these lie property dualism, which grants that there is only physical substance but insists that it has irreducibly mental properties, and idealism, the bold thesis defended by George Berkeley that reality is ultimately mental and that matter, apart from being perceived, is nothing at all. The central difficulty for any purely physical account is what David Chalmers named the hard problem of consciousness. Even a complete physical and functional description of the brain, explaining how it processes information, controls behaviour and reports its own states, seems to leave a residue unexplained: why is there something it is like to undergo these processes, why are they accompanied by subjective experience at all rather than proceeding in the dark? One can imagine, the argument goes, a being physically identical to a conscious person but lacking any inner experience, a philosophical zombie, and the very conceivability of such a being suggests that consciousness is not logically guaranteed by the physical facts. Materialists reply in many ways, some denying that zombies are genuinely conceivable, some arguing that our sense of an explanatory gap reflects the peculiar way we know our own minds rather than any gap in nature, and some biting the bullet with eliminativism, the claim that our commonsense picture of the mind is simply mistaken. The problem remains unsolved, a place where metaphysics, neuroscience and the philosophy of mind meet without yet agreeing.

sections.heading: Criticisms, Skeptics and Metaphysics Today
sections.body: Metaphysics has always had its critics, and the recurring charge is that its questions are unanswerable, that its disputes make no progress, and that its grand systems float free of any check against reality. The empiricist David Hume gave the complaint memorable form with his fork, dividing all genuine knowledge into relations of ideas, such as mathematics, and matters of fact, established by experience. Any book of metaphysics that contains neither, he wrote, should be committed to the flames, for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion. This challenge, that metaphysical claims are neither provable by reason alone nor testable by observation, has echoed ever since and forces the metaphysician to say what kind of inquiry, if any, they are conducting. Immanuel Kant delivered a subtler critique in his Critique of Pure Reason. He argued that human reason inevitably reaches beyond the bounds of possible experience when it tries to grasp the world as it is in itself, and that when it does so it falls into contradiction. His antinomies displayed pairs of opposed conclusions, that the world both must and cannot have a beginning in time, for instance, each apparently provable, showing reason at war with itself. Kant did not abandon metaphysics but relocated it: we cannot know things in themselves, only appearances structured by our own forms of intuition and categories of understanding, so a legitimate metaphysics becomes the study of the necessary framework of experience rather than of a reality beyond it. In the twentieth century the logical positivists of the Vienna Circle, wielding the verification principle that a statement is meaningful only if it can be empirically tested or is true by definition, went further and dismissed metaphysical assertions as literally meaningless, neither true nor false but nonsense. Rudolf Carnap argued that many metaphysical disputes were merely disagreements about which language to adopt, masquerading as disputes about the world. Yet metaphysics survived and revived, partly because the positivists' own verification principle proved unable to pass its own test and could not be stated without self-refutation, and partly through the work of Quine, who tore down the sharp boundary between analytic and synthetic truths and argued that ontological questions are continuous with science rather than separate from it. The later twentieth century saw a vigorous renaissance of analytic metaphysics, armed with the tools of modern logic and the modal insights of Kripke and Lewis, addressing causation, time, persistence and possibility with new rigour. Critics remain, including advocates of naturalized metaphysics who insist that speculation be disciplined by and answerable to physics. But the perennial questions, what exists, what reality is fundamentally like, have proven impossible to abolish, arising anew whenever thinkers, including scientists interpreting their own theories, push their inquiries to the bottom. Metaphysics endures because, however hard its questions, they will not go away.

guides.title: What Is Philosophy — Questions, Methods and Why It Matters
guides.summary: An introduction to philosophy as a discipline: the questions it asks, its main branches, the methods it uses to reason, its major historical traditions, and why it remains useful.

sections.heading: Defining Philosophy: The Love of Wisdom
sections.body: The word philosophy comes from the Greek philosophia, meaning "love of wisdom," a term traditionally attributed to Pythagoras, who is said to have modestly called himself not a wise man but a lover of wisdom. That etymology captures something real: philosophy is less a fixed body of doctrine than an activity, the disciplined and self-critical pursuit of understanding about the most general and fundamental features of reality, knowledge, value and reasoning. What distinguishes philosophical questions from others is their depth and generality. A biologist asks how a particular organism functions; a philosopher asks what it is for anything to be alive, or conscious, or a person. A physicist measures how objects move through time; a philosopher asks what time itself is, and whether the past and future exist. A judge applies laws; a philosopher asks what makes a law just, and whether we have any genuine obligation to obey. Philosophy tends to begin where the assumptions of ordinary life and of the special sciences run out—at the questions those disciplines must presuppose but cannot themselves answer. A useful way to see its scope is that philosophy examines the concepts we use to think at all: existence, cause, mind, meaning, truth, goodness, justice, freedom, beauty. These are ideas so basic that we rarely notice we are relying on them, and philosophy makes them the explicit object of inquiry. Because its questions are so general, philosophy cannot usually settle them by observation or experiment alone; its primary instruments are argument, analysis and reflection, the careful construction and testing of reasons. This gives the subject a distinctive character. It rarely reaches the kind of settled consensus that marks the mature natural sciences, and its central questions have been debated for over two and a half thousand years without final resolution. That is sometimes taken as a mark of failure, but it more accurately reflects the difficulty and depth of the problems and the fact that, historically, whenever a philosophical field does develop rigorous methods of settling its questions, it tends to spin off and become a separate science—as physics, psychology, economics and logic all once did within philosophy. What remains behind is the hard residue of genuinely open questions. Philosophy is also reflexive in a way few other subjects are: one of its enduring questions is what philosophy itself is and whether it makes progress, so the discipline continually turns its methods on itself. To do philosophy well is not to memorise the opinions of great thinkers but to think through the problems oneself, weighing arguments, considering objections, and following the reasoning wherever it leads, even to uncomfortable conclusions. The tradition of named thinkers—Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, and countless others—matters chiefly because their arguments remain worth engaging, not because their authority settles anything. Philosophy, in short, is the ongoing, communal attempt to think clearly and honestly about questions that matter and that resist easy answers.

sections.heading: The Core Questions and How Philosophy Divides Its Labour
sections.body: Although philosophy addresses an enormous range of problems, its questions cluster around a handful of very general concerns, and the discipline has traditionally organised itself into branches according to which concern is central. The oldest and most influential division recognises three or four principal fields. Metaphysics asks what there is and what it is like—what kinds of things exist, what the world is fundamentally made of, and what notions such as time, cause, identity and possibility really involve. Epistemology asks about knowledge and justified belief—what we can know, how we can know it, what distinguishes knowledge from mere opinion, and how far scepticism can be answered. Ethics, or moral philosophy, asks how we ought to live and act—what makes actions right or wrong, what is genuinely good for a human being, and what we owe to one another. Logic studies the principles of valid reasoning itself, the forms of argument that preserve truth, and is in a sense the toolkit the other branches use. Around this core lie further fields defined by their subject matter. Political philosophy examines the state, justice, authority, rights and liberty. Aesthetics investigates beauty, art and taste. The philosophy of mind studies consciousness, thought and the relation of mental states to the physical brain. The philosophy of science asks what science is, how theories are confirmed, and what its findings tell us about reality. The philosophy of language analyses meaning, reference and communication. There are philosophies of mathematics, of religion, of history, of law, of biology, and of almost every human activity, each subjecting the assumptions of its field to scrutiny. A different but complementary way to divide the labour is by the kind of question asked. Some questions are metaphysical, about what exists; some epistemological, about what we can know; some normative, about how things ought to be as opposed to how they merely are; and some conceptual or logical, about the meaning and coherence of our ideas. The distinction between the descriptive and the normative—between is and ought—is especially important, and confusing them, as the philosopher David Hume warned, is a persistent source of error. These divisions are conveniences rather than rigid walls, because the deepest problems refuse to respect them. A question in ethics about free will and responsibility quickly becomes a metaphysical question about determinism; a question in epistemology about whether we can know the external world is inseparable from metaphysical questions about what that world is. The branches are best understood as overlapping perspectives on a single connected web of problems, and one of the pleasures and difficulties of the subject is that pulling seriously on any one thread soon brings the others into play.
